text: Foundations covered the one-page business case that gets a pilot funded. That document's whole job is to win a first yes. Once the pilot proves itself and the program scales, that one-time ask is gone — something else has to keep the money flowing every budget cycle after that.

Many programs start as a funded project with a start date, an end date, and a personal champion. That works for a pilot, but it doesn't survive year two unless the program converts to a run-rate budget — an ongoing operating line renewed like payroll, not re-pitched from scratch every twelve months.

Defending that budget takes a value realization report, built from the same KPIs covered in Chapter 3: value actually delivered against the original promise, the cost of not having the program framed for the specific audience, and what's different this cycle. Proving the existing ask already paid off is the argument — new asks get their own scoped case.

When a budget gets cut anyway, the roadmap's now, next, later structure makes the conversation survivable — naming exactly what stays, what slips, and what waits. And when a sponsor leaves, spreading sponsorship across the council before it's tested is what keeps the renewal from depending on one person's memory.

A sustaining program defends the budget it already has with evidence, not a fresh pitch — and protects itself from both a bad quarter and a departed champion by spreading the case and the sponsorship across more than one person. Next: assessing how mature the program actually is.
